newsitem.title: USA: U.S. delays action against EU meat; averts trade war.
newsitem.headline: U.S. delays action against EU meat; averts trade war.

text.p: The United States extended its deadline on Tuesday for taking action against meat imports from the European Union and averted a potentially nasty and expensive trade war, at least for a while.

Paul Drazek, senior trade adviser to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and head U.S. negotiator at the ongoing bilateral talks on the dispute, announced that Washington would delay until April 30 its plan to take more than 100 European meat and poultry packing plants off its list of approved exporters, in hopes that the increasingly bitter fight between the EU and the United States over meat inspection rules can be settled.
The threatened action by Washington could halt the flow of up to $300 million worth of EU meat shipments to the United States, mostly pork products from Denmark and Italian ham.

EU negotiators return to Washington Wednesday to continue the so-called veterinary equivalency talks. Negotiators ended face-to-face talks last Friday and kept in contact over the weekend through faxes and phone calls.
Drazek said new proposals were made over the weekend and that negotiators would be gathering together again "for further elaboration of these ideas."

Since April 1, U.S. poultry exports to Europe have been blocked because of new inspection regulations imposed by the EU. Some $50 million worth of U.S. poultry is shipped every year to the European Union.

The new rules were introduced after the failure of the two sides to reach agreement in talks that began three years ago after the end of the Uruguay Round of negotiations under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.

Poultry issues have remained the key sticking points in the negotiations. While progress has reportedly been made in several other non-poultry areas, U.S. and EU officials still are in disagreement over how the U.S. poultry industry decontaminates carcasses with a chlorine solution
The U.S. poultry industry welcomed the latest development in the difficult talks and said it was hopeful that a settlement can be worked out in the next two weeks.

"As long as the negotiations continue, there's reason to be optimistic that the unresolved poultry issues will be resolved," said Bill Roenigk, senior vice president of the National Broiler Council. "The fact that we have good strong negotiators gives us reason to be hopeful."
But sources said it will not be easy to settle the dispute, and noted that both sides still appear to be fairly entrenched in their positions.

In the poultry disagreement, which officials have said is the major obstacle remaining, Roenigk strongly defended the U.S. poultry industry's practice of using chlorine as a decontaminant, and said that since it has been proven perfectly safe, there is no reason to stop using it.
"It's safe, it's economical. Why should we be told arbitrarily by the Europeans to give it up?" said Roenigk.
Many U.S. meat industry sources had anticipated Monday that Washington would avert a full-blown trade war with Europe by accepting a deal on everything except the poultry issues.
The U.S. poultry industry had warned this would be unacceptable and that it would not support such a decision.

The EU recently proposed to undertake a scientific study with Washington on decontaminants in the slaughter and packing process, but did not include chlorine in the proposed study. U.S. negotiators said they were studying the plan, but have expressed concern about excluding chlorine.
The talks have covered a wide range of issues and sectors -- including the beef and pork industry, the poultry industry, the pet food sector and the dairy and egg sectors.
